statement: In children and adolescents with ADHD (9 small studies with 246 young people, mostly boys, average ages about 8 to 12 years; a meta-analysis searched to March 2015; Kidwell et al., 2015), nights on stimulant medicine (methylphenidate in 6 studies; amphetamine-type medicines, including lisdexamfetamine and mixed amphetamine salts, in 3) compared with nights without it are associated with taking longer to fall asleep (standardized difference 0.78, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.02; 0.54, 0.28 to 0.81, after a correction for possibly missing studies; 7 studies, 171 young people), less efficient sleep (−0.39, −0.69 to −0.08; −0.32 after correction; 7 studies) and shorter sleep (−0.59, −0.84 to −0.35; 7 studies, 223 young people), measured with wrist activity monitors or overnight sleep recordings. Differences between studies were large (I² 67% to 83%), and the review gives no results in minutes. Although it included only studies with random assignment, it compared medicated nights mostly with nights before treatment began (placebo nights in 4 studies), converted some results using an assumed correlation, and did not report the trials' risk of bias. Comparing studies with each other, the effect on sleep efficiency was smaller where children had taken the medicine for more days, which does not show that a child's sleep adapts. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In 9 studies of children and teenagers with ADHD who wore sleep monitors, nights on stimulant medicine (methylphenidate or amphetamine-type medicines) were compared with nights without it. On medicine, they took longer to fall asleep, slept less, and their sleep was less efficient. The review does not say by how many minutes. The effect on sleep efficiency looked smaller in studies where children had taken the medicine for longer, but that comparison between studies cannot show that sleep gets better with time.
population: Children and adolescents with ADHD (mean ages about 8.5 to 11.6 years; 42% to 85% boys) in 9 small studies with random assignment to stimulant conditions and actigraphy or polysomnography
exposure: Nights on prescribed stimulant medicine: methylphenidate (6 studies) or amphetamine-class medicines, including lisdexamfetamine and mixed amphetamine salts (3 studies); study conditions in the study card
comparator: The same children's unmedicated nights: mostly pre-treatment baseline nights, placebo nights in 4 studies
outcome: Sleep latency, sleep efficiency and total sleep time measured by actigraphy or polysomnography
magnitude: Hedges' g (random effects): sleep latency 0.78 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.02), I² 67.30%, after trim-and-fill 0.54 (0.28 to 0.81); sleep efficiency −0.39 (−0.69 to −0.08), I² 83.37%, after trim-and-fill −0.32 (−0.63 to −0.01); total sleep time −0.59 (−0.84 to −0.35), I² 82.67%, no asymmetry. No differences in minutes are reported.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Methods › Study Selection (p. 2); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 5)
evidence.extracted: Nine studies with 246 young people were included from 9927 records and 167 full texts; eligibility required random assignment to stimulant conditions and actigraphy or polysomnography; studies were collected through March 2015.

evidence.locator: Methods › Data Extraction; Effect Size Calculation
evidence.extracted: Effect sizes compared baseline with medicated sleep, with placebo nights used where a study gave no baseline (4 studies), and a correlation of 0.5 was assumed when the needed statistics were missing.

evidence.locator: Results › The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Sleep Latency, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Sleep latency, 7 samples (N = 171): g = 0.78 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.02), I² 67.30%; after trim-and-fill with 3 imputed studies, 0.54 (0.28 to 0.81).

evidence.locator: Results › The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Sleep Efficiency
evidence.extracted: Sleep efficiency, 7 samples (N = 155): g = −0.39 (−0.69 to −0.08), I² 83.37%; after trim-and-fill with 1 imputed study, −0.32 (−0.63 to −0.01); the negative effect was smaller in studies with more days on medication (b = 0.05 per day).

evidence.locator: Results › The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Total Sleep Time
evidence.extracted: Total sleep time, 7 samples (N = 223): g = −0.59 (−0.84 to −0.35), I² 82.67%, with no funnel-plot asymmetry and no significant moderators.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (read on the rendered, rotated page)
evidence.extracted: Single-study effects: sleep latency 0.44 to 1.15, all longer on medication; sleep efficiency −1.76 to 0.48, one study better on medication; total sleep −1.31 to −0.16, all shorter; mean ages 102 to 139.2 months.

The authors note that publication bias was present for latency and efficiency, that the correction may underestimate effects and that moderator results rest on few studies; there was no external funding.

risk_of_bias.note: The pooled contrasts are mostly medicated against pre-treatment nights rather than the randomized placebo contrast; the trials' risk of bias was not reported; correlations were assumed; two samples may overlap.

inconsistency.note: I² 67% to 83%, but sleep onset and total sleep point the same way in every study, and efficiency in six of seven.

indirectness.note: Worded for prescribed use in young people with ADHD.

imprecision.note: Intervals exclude no effect for all three outcomes.

publication_bias.note: Funnel asymmetry for latency and efficiency (studies imputed by trim-and-fill); published studies only.

grade.reasoning: Studies with random assignment start high, but the pooled contrasts are mostly within-child comparisons with pre-treatment nights. Risk of bias −1 and publication bias −1 give low. Status replicated: every study found longer sleep onset and shorter sleep on medication. This complements the meta-analysis of reported sleep problems in placebo-controlled methylphenidate trials (Faraone et al., 2019), which draws on a partly overlapping literature.
